claim: The genome and gene repertoire of the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA) was likely small relative to that of most extant eukaryotic organisms
source: Given that the genome and gene repertoire of the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA) was likely small relative to that of most extant eukaryotic organisms (Becerra et al., 2007; Goldman et al., 2013) (Figure 1A), what processes gave rise to these distinct gene families?
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Becerra et al., 2007 and Goldman et al., 2013

claim: About 5% of the ~500 identified yeast paralogue pairs resulting from whole genome duplication had very weak or no similarity at all
source: An example of this was found when examining yeast duplicates resulting from whole genome duplication (WGD) where it was reported that about 5% of the ~500 identified paralogue pairs had very weak or no similarity at all (Wolfe, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wolfe, 2004

claim: Divergence was considered to be the only realistic evolutionary explanation for the origin of new gene families for a long time
source: For a long time, divergence was considered to be the only realistic evolutionary explanation for the origin of new gene families (Long et al., 2003), while de novo emergence has only recently been appreciated as a widespread phenomenon (Van Oss and Carvunis, 2019; Carvunis et al., 2012; Long et al., 2013; Tautz, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Long et al., 2003 and other references

claim: De novo emergence has only recently been appreciated as a widespread phenomenon
source: For a long time, divergence was considered to be the only realistic evolutionary explanation for the origin of new gene families (Long et al., 2003), while de novo emergence has only recently been appreciated as a widespread phenomenon (Van Oss and Carvunis, 2019; Carvunis et al., 2012; Long et al., 2013; Tautz, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Van Oss and Carvunis, 2019; Carvunis et al., 2012; Long et al., 2013; Tautz, 2014

claim: Complete divergence accounts, on average, for at most a third of eukaryotic orphan and taxonomically restricted genes
source: By separately comparing yeast, fly and human genes to related taxa using conservative criteria, we find that complete divergence accounts, on average, for at most a third of eukaryotic orphan and taxonomically restricted genes.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 6

claim: Complete divergence occurs at a stable rate within a phylum but at different rates between phyla
source: We observe that complete divergence occurs at a stable rate within a phylum but at different rates between phyla, and is frequently associated with gene shortening akin to pseudogenization.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis presented in Figure 4 showing linear correlations within phyla with different slopes

claim: Complete divergence is frequently associated with gene shortening akin to pseudogenization
source: We observe that complete divergence occurs at a stable rate within a phylum but at different rates between phyla, and is frequently associated with gene shortening akin to pseudogenization.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis presented in Figure 8B showing focal genes tend to be much shorter than their undetectable homologues

claim: Genes found in conserved syntenic positions in a pair of genomes will usually share ancestry
source: The central idea behind our pipeline is that genes found in conserved syntenic positions in a pair of genomes will usually share ancestry.
evidence: This is a methodological assumption based on established principles of comparative genomics

claim: The same basic principle of using synteny has been previously used to detect pairs of WGD paralogues in yeast
source: The same basic principle has been previously used to detect pairs of WGD paralogues in yeast (Wolfe and Shields, 1997; Kellis et al., 2004; Dietrich, 2004) and more recently to identify homologous long non-coding RNAs (Herrera-Úbeda et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wolfe and Shields, 1997; Kellis et al., 2004; Dietrich, 2004

claim: The synteny-based principle has been used to identify homologous long non-coding RNAs
source: The same basic principle has been previously used to detect pairs of WGD paralogues in yeast (Wolfe and Shields, 1997; Kellis et al., 2004; Dietrich, 2004) and more recently to identify homologous long non-coding RNAs (Herrera-Úbeda et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Herrera-Úbeda et al., 2019

claim: 180 unique focal species genes in yeast have at least one undetectable homologue in at least one target species but no significant sequence similarity
source: In total, we were able to identify 180, 81 and 156 unique focal species genes in the dataset of yeast, fly and human respectively, that have at least one undetectable homologue in at least one target species but no significant sequence similarity to that homologue or to any other part of the target genome (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for two exemplars of these findings).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis results from the synteny-based pipeline

claim: 81 unique focal species genes in fly have at least one undetectable homologue in at least one target species but no significant sequence similarity
source: In total, we were able to identify 180, 81 and 156 unique focal species genes in the dataset of yeast, fly and human respectively, that have at least one undetectable homologue in at least one target species but no significant sequence similarity to that homologue or to any other part of the target genome (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for two exemplars of these findings).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis results from the synteny-based pipeline

claim: 156 unique focal species genes in human have at least one undetectable homologue in at least one target species but no significant sequence similarity
source: In total, we were able to identify 180, 81 and 156 unique focal species genes in the dataset of yeast, fly and human respectively, that have at least one undetectable homologue in at least one target species but no significant sequence similarity to that homologue or to any other part of the target genome (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for two exemplars of these findings).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis results from the synteny-based pipeline

claim: Within phyla, the proportion of putative undetectable homologues correlated strongly with time since divergence
source: Within phyla, the proportion of putative undetectable homologues correlated strongly with time since divergence, suggesting a continuous process acting during evolution (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 4 with linear fits

claim: Different rates of divergence beyond recognition were observed between phyla
source: However, different rates were observed between phyla, represented by the slopes of the fitted linear models in Figure 4.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 4 comparing slopes across datasets

claim: Genes appeared to be diverging beyond recognition at a faster pace in the yeast and fly lineages than in the human lineage
source: Genes appeared to be diverging beyond recognition at a faster pace in the yeast and fly lineages than in the human lineage.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of slopes in Figure 4

claim: The distributions of dS are statistically indistinguishable for genes inside and outside of micro-synteny regions in the yeast and fly datasets
source: The distributions of dS are statistically indistinguishable for genes inside and outside of micro-synteny regions in the yeast and fly datasets.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of dS distributions shown in Figure 5A

claim: The distributions of dN for all three datasets show a statistically significant increase in genes outside conserved micro-synteny regions compared to genes inside such regions, but the effect size is minimal
source: The distributions of dN for all three datasets and dS for the human dataset show a statistically significant increase in genes outside conserved micro-synteny regions compared to genes inside such regions, but the effect size is minimal, almost negligible (Rosenthal's R ~ 0.05, Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B with effect size calculations

claim: The estimated contribution of divergence to genes without similarity ranges from 0% in D. sechellia to 57% in T. castaneum, with an overall average of 20.6%
source: The estimated contribution of divergence ranges from 0% in the case of D. sechellia (fly dataset), to 57% in the case of T. castaneum (fly dataset), with an overall average of 20.6% (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: In most pairwise species comparisons, the observed proportion of all genes without similarity far exceeds that estimated to have originated by divergence
source: We found that, in most pairwise species comparisons, the observed proportion of all genes without similarity far exceeds that estimated to have originated by divergence (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 6A comparing solid and transparent bars

claim: The proportion of TRGs which originated by divergence-beyond-recognition at the level of Saccharomyces is at most 45%
source: We estimate that the proportion of TRGs which originated by divergence-beyond-recognition, at the level of Saccharomyces, melanogaster subgroup, and primates are at most 45%, 20% and 24%, respectively (Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on phylogeny-based analysis described in Materials and methods

claim: The proportion of TRGs which originated by divergence-beyond-recognition at the level of melanogaster subgroup is at most 20%
source: We estimate that the proportion of TRGs which originated by divergence-beyond-recognition, at the level of Saccharomyces, melanogaster subgroup, and primates are at most 45%, 20% and 24%, respectively (Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on phylogeny-based analysis described in Materials and methods

claim: The proportion of TRGs which originated by divergence-beyond-recognition at the level of primates is at most 24%
source: We estimate that the proportion of TRGs which originated by divergence-beyond-recognition, at the level of Saccharomyces, melanogaster subgroup, and primates are at most 45%, 20% and 24%, respectively (Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on phylogeny-based analysis described in Materials and methods

claim: The origin of most genes without similarity cannot be attributed to divergence beyond recognition
source: Thus, we conclude that the origin of most genes without similarity cannot be attributed to divergence beyond recognition.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing divergence accounts for at most a third of orphans and TRGs

claim: There is a substantial role for other evolutionary mechanisms such as de novo emergence and horizontal gene transfer in the origin of genes without similarity
source: This implies a substantial role for other evolutionary mechanisms such as de novo emergence and horizontal gene transfer, although horizontal gene transfer is not known to be frequent in metazoa.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that divergence does not explain most orphans and TRGs

claim: Horizontal gene transfer is not known to be frequent in metazoa
source: This implies a substantial role for other evolutionary mechanisms such as de novo emergence and horizontal gene transfer, although horizontal gene transfer is not known to be frequent in metazoa.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Weak but significant correlations exist between pairs of undetectable homologues in the human dataset when comparing G+C content (Spearman's rho = 0.25, p-value=2×10−5)
source: We found weak but significant correlations between pairs of undetectable homologues in the human dataset when comparing G+C content (Spearman's rho = 0.25, p-value=2×10−5) and CDS length (Spearman's rho = 0.35, p-value=1.5×10−9).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of undetectable homologue pairs

claim: Weak but significant correlations exist between pairs of undetectable homologues in the human dataset when comparing CDS length (Spearman's rho = 0.35, p-value=1.5×10−9)
source: We found weak but significant correlations between pairs of undetectable homologues in the human dataset when comparing G+C content (Spearman's rho = 0.25, p-value=2×10−5) and CDS length (Spearman's rho = 0.35, p-value=1.5×10−9).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of undetectable homologue pairs

claim: In the yeast and human dataset, focal proteins had significantly fewer Pfam matches than their undetectable homologues
source: We searched for shared Pfam (Finn et al., 2016) domains (protein functional motifs) and found that, in the yeast and human dataset, focal proteins had significantly fewer Pfam matches than their undetectable homologues (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: A common Pfam match between undetectable homologues was found only for 12 pairs out of a total of 845 examined (1.4%)
source: Overall, a common Pfam match between undetectable homologues was found only for 12 pairs out of a total of 845 that we examined (1.4%).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis of Pfam domain matches

claim: 13 additional cases of undetectable homologue pairs belonged to the same OrthoDB group despite not sharing any pairwise similarity
source: We also identified 13 additional cases of undetectable homologue pairs that, despite not sharing any pairwise similarity, belonged to the same OrthoDB group.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis using OrthoDB groupings

claim: Genes forming the 25 pairs with common Pfam domains or OrthoDB groups were strongly correlated across 9 out of 10 features tested
source: Nonetheless, and despite the small sample size, genes forming these 25 pairs (corresponding to 17 distinct focal genes) were strongly correlated across 9 out of 10 features tested (Bonferroni-corrected P-values of <0.05; see Figure 7B and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B

claim: MNE1 is a 1992nt long S. cerevisiae gene encoding a protein that is a component of the mitochondrial splicing apparatus
source: One of these rare cases is MNE1, a 1992nt long S. cerevisiae gene encoding a protein that is a component of the mitochondrial splicing apparatus (Watts et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Watts et al., 2011

claim: MNE1 of S. cerevisiae has no detectable protein or genomic similarity to its homologous gene in Kluyveromyces lactis, KLLA0_F23485g
source: In four of the five species the homologue can also be identified by sequence similarity, but MNE1 of S. cerevisiae has no detectable protein or genomic similarity to its homologous gene in Kluyveromyces lactis, KLLA0_F23485g.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis from the synteny-based pipeline

claim: Despite the lack of primary sequence similarity, the S. cerevisiae and K. lactis MNE1 genes share a significant (E-value <0.001) Pfam match
source: Despite the lack of primary sequence similarity, the S. cerevisiae and K. lactis genes share a significant (E-value <0.001) Pfam match (Pfam accession PF13762.5; Figure 7C) and are members of the same fast-evolving OrthoDB group (EOG092E0K2I).
evidence: The claim is based on Pfam domain analysis shown in Figure 7C

claim: Focal genes resulting from complete lineage-specific divergence tend to be much shorter than their undetectable homologues
source: When comparing the CDS lengths of these focal genes to those of their undetectable homologues, we found that focal genes tend to be much shorter (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 8B

claim: The shorter lengths frequently associated with young genes could be partially explained by gene truncation during divergence
source: This finding could partially explain the shorter lengths frequently associated with young genes (Vakirlis et al., 2018; Carvunis et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2017; Ruiz-Orera et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data on gene length and supported by citations

claim: YLR255C is a 354nt long, uncharacterized yeast ORF that is conserved across S. cerevisiae strains
source: YLR255C is a 354nt long, uncharacterized yeast ORF that is conserved across S. cerevisiae strains according to the Saccharomyces Genome Database (Cherry et al., 2012) (SGD).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cherry et al., 2012 (SGD)

claim: YLR255C is a species-specific, orphan gene
source: YLR255C is a species-specific, orphan gene.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis from the synteny-based pipeline

claim: The presence of two orphan genes in conserved synteny is strong evidence for extensive sequence divergence as an explanation of their origin
source: The presence of two orphan genes in conserved synteny is strong evidence for extensive sequence divergence as an explanation of their origin.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the synteny data

claim: Thirteen human genes underwent complete divergence along the human lineage and have no detectable homologues outside of mammals
source: Our approach identified thirteen human genes that underwent complete divergence along the human lineage and have no detectable homologues outside of mammals (see Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis from the synteny-based pipeline

claim: Three out of thirteen human genes that underwent complete divergence are associated with known phenotypes
source: Examining the ENSEMBL and UniProt resources revealed that three of these thirteen genes are associated with known phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is based on database searches in ENSEMBL and UniProt

claim: MT-ATP8 has been implicated with infantile cardiomyopathy
source: One of them is ATP-synthase membrane subunit 8 (MT-ATP8), which has been implicated with infantile cardiomyopathy (Ware et al., 2009) and Kearns-Sayre syndrome (van der Westhuizen et al., 2010) among other diseases.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ware et al., 2009

claim: MT-ATP8 has been implicated with Kearns-Sayre syndrome
source: One of them is ATP-synthase membrane subunit 8 (MT-ATP8), which has been implicated with infantile cardiomyopathy (Ware et al., 2009) and Kearns-Sayre syndrome (van der Westhuizen et al., 2010) among other diseases.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to van der Westhuizen et al., 2010

claim: DEC1 is associated with cancer
source: The other two are both associated with cancer: DEC1 (Nishiwaki et al., 2000) and DIRC1 (Druck et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nishiwaki et al., 2000

claim: DIRC1 is associated with cancer
source: The other two are both associated with cancer: DEC1 (Nishiwaki et al., 2000) and DIRC1 (Druck et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Druck et al., 2001

claim: Multiple novel human genes are associated with cancer and cancer outcomes suggesting a role for antagonistic evolution in the origin of new genes
source: Nonetheless, this observation is consistent with previous findings showing that multiple novel human genes are associated with cancer and cancer outcomes suggesting a role for antagonistic evolution in the origin of new genes (McLysaght and Hurst, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McLysaght and Hurst, 2016

claim: Sequence divergence of ancestral genes explains only a minority of orphans and TRGs
source: Here, we have specifically addressed this problem and demonstrated that sequence divergence of ancestral genes explains only a minority of orphans and TRGs.
evidence: The claim is based on the overall findings from the data analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: In yeast and in Arabidopsis, ~50% of orphan genes are located outside of syntenic regions of near relatives
source: Since, for example, in yeast and in Arabidopsis,~50% of orphan genes are located outside of syntenic regions of near relatives (Arendsee et al., 2019), the study of their evolutionary origins represents exciting challenges for future work.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Arendsee et al., 2019

claim: Generation time and/or population size may affect evolutionary rates and thereby the process of complete divergence
source: One potential explanation is an effect of generation time and/or population size on evolutionary rates (Martin and Palumbi, 1993; Bromham and Penny, 2003) and thereby on the process of complete divergence.
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to Martin and Palumbi, 1993; Bromham and Penny, 2003

claim: Orphan genes and TRGs can be the result of divergence of pre-existing genes
source: By definition, orphan genes and TRGs can be the result of two processes. The first process is divergence of pre-existing genes (Tautz and Domazet-Lošo, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tautz and Domazet-Lošo, 2011

claim: Orphan genes and TRGs can be the result of de novo emergence from previously non-genic sequences
source: The second process is de novo emergence from previously non-genic sequences (Vakirlis et al., 2018; McLysaght and Guerzoni, 2015; Van Oss and Carvunis, 2019) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vakirlis et al., 2018; McLysaght and Guerzoni, 2015; Van Oss and Carvunis, 2019

claim: De novo emergence has a high potential to produce entirely unique genes
source: De novo emergence is thought to have a high potential to produce entirely unique genes (Schlötterer, 2015) (though examples of convergent selection exist, see Baalsrud et al., 2018; Zhuang et al., 2019), whereas divergence, being more gradual, can stop before this occurs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schlötterer, 2015

claim: Examples of convergent selection in de novo gene emergence exist
source: De novo emergence is thought to have a high potential to produce entirely unique genes (Schlötterer, 2015) (though examples of convergent selection exist, see Baalsrud et al., 2018; Zhuang et al., 2019), whereas divergence, being more gradual, can stop before this occurs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baalsrud et al., 2018; Zhuang et al., 2019

claim: For the vast majority of focal genes examined that do have matches, the match occurs in the predicted region within the region of conserved micro-synteny
source: We find that, for the vast majority of focal genes examined that do have matches, the match occurs in the predicted region ('opposite'), that is within the region of conserved micro-synteny. In 36/48 pair-wise species comparisons, at least 90% of the focal genes in micro-synteny for which at least one match was eventually found in the target genome, a match was within the predicted micro-syntenic region (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: In 36/48 pair-wise species comparisons, at least 90% of the focal genes in micro-synteny for which at least one match was found had a match within the predicted micro-syntenic region
source: In 36/48 pair-wise species comparisons, at least 90% of the focal genes in micro-synteny for which at least one match was eventually found in the target genome, a match was within the predicted micro-syntenic region (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: The finding that matches occur in predicted regions supports the soundness of the synteny-based approach for homologue identification
source: This finding supports the soundness of our synteny-based approach for homologue identification.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing high proportion of matches in predicted regions

claim: The phylostratigraphy optimal E-value thresholds are 0.01 for all comparisons using yeast and fly as focal species
source: The phylostratigraphy optimal E-value thresholds are 0.01 for all comparisons using yeast and fly as focal species and 0.001 for those of human, except for chimpanzee (10−4).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis optimizing E-value thresholds

claim: The phylostratigraphy optimal E-value threshold is 0.001 for human comparisons, except for chimpanzee (10−4)
source: The phylostratigraphy optimal E-value thresholds are 0.01 for all comparisons using yeast and fly as focal species and 0.001 for those of human, except for chimpanzee (10−4).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis optimizing E-value thresholds

claim: The optimal E-value cut-offs for identifying orphan genes in Drosophila were previously estimated to be in the range of 10−3 - 10−5
source: These are close to previously estimated optimal E-value cut-offs for identifying orphan genes in Drosophila, found in the range of 10−3 - 10−5, see ref (Domazet-Loso and Tautz, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Domazet-Loso and Tautz, 2003

claim: The proportion of undetectable homologies depended quasi-linearly on the E-value cut-off
source: The proportion of undetectable homologies depended quasi-linearly on the E-value cut-off.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: False homologies depended exponentially on the E-value cut-off
source: By contrast, false homologies depended exponentially on the cut-off, as expected from the E-value definition.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 3A and expected from E-value definition

claim: The impact of E-value cut-off was more pronounced in comparisons of species separated by longer evolutionary distances
source: Furthermore, the impact of E-value cut-off was more pronounced in comparisons of species separated by longer evolutionary distances, whereas it was almost non-existent for comparisons amongst the most closely related species.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: There is no dependence between percentage of false homologies and evolutionary time across the range of E-values tested
source: Conversely, there seems to be no dependence between percentage of false homologies and evolutionary time across the range of E-values that we have tested (all lines overlap in the graphs in the bottom panel of Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: When comparing relatively closely related species, failing to appropriately control for false homologies would have an overall more severe effect on homology detection than failing to account for false negatives
source: This means that, when comparing relatively closely related species, failing to appropriately control for false homologies would have an overall more severe effect on homology detection than failing to account for false negatives.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data on false homologies and E-value dependence

claim: Homology detection is highly sensitive to the technical choices made during sequence similarity searches
source: Homology detection is highly sensitive to the technical choices made during sequence similarity searches (Tautz and Domazet-Lošo, 2011; Arendsee et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tautz and Domazet-Lošo, 2011; Arendsee et al., 2019

claim: Biological sequences do not evolve by reversal
source: Matches produced in these searches can safely be considered 'false homologies' since biological sequences do not evolve by reversal (Frith, 2011) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Frith, 2011

claim: The estimates from the synteny-based pipeline can be viewed as an upper bound estimate of the true rate of divergence beyond recognition
source: The estimates that we will provide of the rate of divergence beyond recognition inside synteny blocks are best viewed as an upper-bound of the true rate because some of the genes found in conserved syntenic positions in a pair of genomes will not be homologous.
evidence: The claim is based on logical reasoning about the limitations of the synteny-based approach

claim: If non-homologous genes in syntenic positions could be removed, the rate of divergence beyond recognition would only decrease, but not increase, relative to the estimate
source: If we could remove all such cases, the rate of divergence beyond recognition would only decrease, but not increase, relative to our estimate (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on logical reasoning illustrated in Figure 2A

claim: With a more stringent conserved synteny definition, the average proportion explained by divergence dropped from 16% to 10.9% in a subset of species
source: A comparison including only species with >200 conserved micro-synteny regions (i.e. excluding 'Vpol', 'Tbla', 'Tpha', 'Ecym', 'Agam', 'Aaeg', 'Bmor', 'Tcas', 'Amel', 'Drer') shows that in the pairwise case the mean drops from 16% in the current one to 10.9% in the stringent one.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B

claim: The annotation used in yeast does not include the vast majority of dubious ORFs
source: Furthermore, the annotation that we used in yeast does not include the vast majority of dubious ORFs, labelled as such because they are not evolutionarily conserved even though most are supported by experimental evidence (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2008

claim: With time, genome rearrangements shuffle genes around and synteny is lost
source: First, with time, genome rearrangements shuffle genes around and synteny is lost.
evidence: This is established knowledge in genomics

claim: Combinations of evolutionary events can place non-homologous genes in directly syntenic positions
source: Second, combinations of evolutionary events can place non-homologous genes in directly syntenic positions. Loss of a gene in a lineage followed by tandem duplication of a neighbouring gene, translocation of a distant one, or de novo emergence, could potentially contribute to placing in syntenic positions pairs of genes that are not in fact homologous.
evidence: This is based on logical reasoning about possible evolutionary scenarios

claim: Previous efforts to measure the rate of complete divergence beyond recognition have used simulations
source: Previous efforts to measure the rate of complete divergence beyond recognition have done so using simulations (Vakirlis et al., 2018; Moyers and Zhang, 2014; Albà and Castresana, 2007; Moyers and Zhang, 2016; Jain et al., 2019), within a different context and with different goals, mainly to measure 'BLAST error'.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple simulation studies

claim: The estimates from this study are of the same order of magnitude as previous results from simulations
source: Interestingly, our estimates are of the same order of magnitude as previous results from simulations (Moyers and Zhang, 2014; Moyers and Zhang, 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with cited simulation studies

claim: Simulation-based studies are limited in that they can only show that sequence divergence could explain a certain proportion of orphans and TRGs, not that it actually does
source: They are however limited in that they can only show that sequence divergence could explain a certain proportion of orphans and TRGs, not that it actually does explain it.
evidence: This is a logical critique of simulation-based approaches

claim: The synteny-based approach does not make assumptions with respect to the evolutionary mechanisms at play
source: Our approach, on the other hand, does not make assumptions with respect to the evolutionary mechanisms at play, that is we do not need prior knowledge of the prevalence of divergence beyond recognition to obtain an estimate.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the approach used in the study

claim: Many studies have previously reported that genes without detectable homologues tended to be shorter than conserved ones
source: Many studies have previously reported that genes without detectable homologues tended to be shorter than conserved ones (Tautz and Domazet-Lošo, 2011; Wissler et al., 2013; Toll-Riera et al., 2009; Ekman and Elofsson, 2010; Palmieri et al., 2014; Vakirlis et al., 2016; Khalturin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The relationship between gene length and lack of homologues has been interpreted as evidence that young genes can arise de novo from short open reading frames
source: This relationship has been interpreted as evidence that young genes can arise de novo from short open reading frames (McLysaght and Guerzoni, 2015; Carvunis et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2014; Siepel, 2009) but also as the result of a bias due to short genes having higher evolutionary rates, which may explain why their homologues are hard to find (Moyers and Zhang, 2014; Moyers and Zhang, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: An event akin to incomplete pseudogenization could be taking place, wherein a gene loses functionality through some disruption, thus triggering rapid divergence due to absence of constraint
source: We have shown that an event akin to incomplete pseudogenization could be taking place, wherein a gene loses functionality through some disruption, thus triggering rapid divergence due to absence of constraint.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data on gene shortening and divergence

claim: After a period of evolutionary 'free fall', gene disruption would eventually lead to an entirely novel sequence
source: After a period of evolutionary 'free fall' (Wolf et al., 2009), this would eventually lead to an entirely novel sequence.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to Wolf et al., 2009

claim: Disentangling complete divergence from other processes of orphan and TRG origination is non-trivial and requires laborious manual inspection
source: Disentangling complete divergence from other processes of orphan and TRG origination is non-trivial and requires laborious manual inspection (Prabh and Rödelsperger, 2019; Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Prabh and Rödelsperger, 2019; Zhou et al., 2008

claim: The findings are consistent with the view that multiple evolutionary processes are responsible for the existence of orphan genes
source: Overall, our findings are consistent with the view that multiple evolutionary processes are responsible for the existence of orphan genes and suggest that, contrary to what has been assumed, divergence is not the predominant one.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the overall data analysis

claim: Contrary to what has been assumed, divergence is not the predominant process responsible for orphan genes
source: Overall, our findings are consistent with the view that multiple evolutionary processes are responsible for the existence of orphan genes and suggest that, contrary to what has been assumed, divergence is not the predominant one.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the data showing divergence accounts for at most a third of orphans
